photograph.author: Diego Delso
photograph.description: Snakelocks anemone ( Anemonia viridis ), Arrábida Natural Park , Portugal. The snakelocks anemone is a predator , related to jellyfish (but without a medusa stage in their lifecycle), that ensnares prey of suitable size that comes within reach of its tentacles immobilizing it with the aid of their nematocysts (explosive cells that contain one giant secretory organelle that can deliver a sting). The prey is then transported to the mouth and thrust into the pharynx. This species is widely consumed in Andalusia and is known as ortiguillas de mar (literally, "little sea nettles", because it has urticant properties before it is cooked). The whole animal is marinated in vinegar , coated in a tempura-like batter , and deep-fried in olive oil .

photograph.author: Diego Delso
photograph.description: Cylinder anemone ( Cerianthus membranaceus ), Arrábida Natural Park , Portugal. This tube-dwelling anemone has an oral disc with a diameter of up to 40 cm (16 in). There are two whorls of tentacles, amounting to about two hundred tentacles in all. Those in the outer whorl are long and slender and armed with cnidocytes (stinging cells) and are used for catching prey. Tentacles in the inner whorl are shorter and function to transfer captured food to the central mouth. This species is found on the seabed in shallow water in the Mediterranean Sea, the northern Adriatic Sea and the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, its range extending as far north as Britain. The tentacles of Cerianthus membranaceus do not retract, but the whole animal can retreat into its tube. As it does so, some of the tentacles grip the rim and pull the tube closed behind it, effectively making it disappear from view. The tube is normally a permanent home, but if the anemone is disturbed from below, as by a burrowing sea urchin, it can eject itself from its tube, move to a new location and secrete a new tube. C. membranaceus feeds on small fish and planktonic organisms which it catches with its tentacles. It is a protandrous hermaphrodite , starting life as a male and becoming a female later. species.title: Smithsonian SERC/NEMESIS orange cup morphology
species.scope: Actual description read with USGS account, plus whole Diego Delso living photograph: orange tissue, yellow tentacles, common coenosteum, 48 internal septa and variable plocoid/phaceloid growth. Smithsonian account is not a collection determination. Source dimensions are not fitted.
species.change: Unequal crowded orange calyces with common basal exterior, selected internal 48-septal relief and mixed short/extended yellow polyp exteriors.
species.problem: The old tall equally spaced orange towers and identical fully extended crowns did not match the photographed colony.
species.limitations: Cup/tissue unions, septal order details, natural variation, full extension/retraction and food handling remain incomplete.
anatomy: Orange calyces and internal septal relief
species.finalScreenshotFindings: Variable short/extended yellow polyps and orange cups are distinct from Cladocora. Common hemisphere and circular packing are too regular; natural coenosteum unions, fleshy rims, irregular cup elevations and local polyp detail remain incomplete.

species.title: Colin et al 2013 cubomedusan propulsion
species.scope: Actual complete PDF pp2-4 including Figures 1-3 and selected methods/captions inspected. Chironex and Chiropsella panels are separated; Figure 6/10 images are Chiropsella, not a Chironex photo. Three consecutive cycles in plotted mean/deviation are not three animals or fitted trajectories. Lewis/Bentlage 2009 selected comparative text was read, but new figure retrieval failed. The separate Australian Museum field photograph credited Gavin Dally was privately inspected and linked only; vitality and photographic identification were not independently redetermined; existing Emoke Denes museum photo is preserved, not live colour/motion evidence.
species.change: Rounder four-sided domed bell, four palmate exterior paddles with separate finger attachments, unequal flattened curved trailing tentacles and a folded open velarium; original subtle spatial pigment and reduced opacity.
species.problem: The previous squared can-like bell, oval knobs, equal near-wire tentacles and dangling egg-like central mouth were oversimplified.
species.limitations: Selected 48 tentacles/twelve per pedalium and ratios are not universal counts or diagnostic identification. Pedalial canal corniculum, fused histology, eye details, natural optics, full swimming, flow/contact forces and feeding remain unresolved.
anatomy: Four pedalia and unequal trailing tentacles
species.finalScreenshotFindings: Rounder four-sided wall, open velarium, palmate attachments and unequal flattened trailing tentacles are visible. Bell/manubrium, rhopalia and pedalial canal detail remain simplified; software opacity obscures fine tissue and the museum reference is preserved, not live-colour evidence.
